prompt: How does object-oriented design differ from the structured techniques of the earlier modules?

options.text: It combines process and data into a single unit called an object
It separates process and data into two unrelated diagrams

explanation: Structured techniques gave two separate views, DFDs for processes and ERDs for data. Object orientation joins them in the object.

why.a: Correct. Process and data in one unit.
why.b: Wrong. That describes the STRUCTURED approach.

prompt: True or false: in object-oriented analysis and design, a running system is a set of objects sending MESSAGES to one another.
explanation: Each object manages its own state and operations, and objects get work done by calling one another's operations.

why.false: Wrong. The text describes the running system exactly so.

prompt: Match each term with its meaning in the course text.

pairs.right: A single instance, such as a particular student
The blueprint objects are created from; holds no data itself
The data an object holds, as attributes
The operations an object can perform, as methods
What distinguishes an object from every other, even with identical attributes

explanation: A class is the blueprint; an object is one instance. Every object has state, behaviour and identity.

prompt: Two students share the same name. Which of the three things every object has keeps them distinct?
explanation: Identity: two students could share a name, but never a student ID.

why.a: Wrong. Their state, the name, is identical here.
why.b: Wrong. They have the same operations.
why.d: Wrong. Inheritance is a relationship between classes, not one of the three things.

prompt: True or false: a class holds the actual data of the objects created from it.
explanation: A class holds NO actual data; it only describes the shape every object of that type follows. The objects hold the data.

why.false: Correct. The class is only the blueprint.

prompt: Match each object-oriented concept with its description.

pairs.right: Data and operations bundled, internal details hidden
A class defined as a specialised version of another
Different classes respond to the same call in their own way

explanation: Encapsulation hides; inheritance reuses; polymorphism lets one call behave differently per class, as calculateFee() does for undergraduates and postgraduates.

prompt: Other parts of a system can interact with an object only through its defined operations, because its internal details are hidden. Which concept is this?
explanation: Encapsulation bundles data with the operations on it and hides the inside.

why.b: Wrong. Polymorphism is one call, many behaviours.

prompt: A Postgraduate Student class takes all the attributes and operations of a general Student class and adds a supervisor. Which concept is this?
explanation: Inheritance: a specialised version reuses the general class and adds its own, avoiding repetition.

why.c: Wrong. Polymorphism is about responding differently to the same call.
why.d: Wrong. Aggregation is a whole-part relationship.

prompt: True or false: with polymorphism, calculateFee() can work differently for an Undergraduate Student and a Postgraduate Student, though both are called the same way.
explanation: That is the text's example: the rest of the system need not know which type it is dealing with.

why.false: Wrong. That is exactly the example given.

prompt: Which two of these are among the six activities of the object-oriented design process?

options.text: Identify the candidate classes, usually from the requirements model
Model how objects interact for each use case, typically with a sequence diagram

explanation: The six: candidate classes; relationships; attributes and operations; class diagram; object interaction per use case (sequence diagram); consistency check against the use cases.

why.b: Wrong. The context diagram belongs to process modelling.
why.c: Correct. Modelling interaction with a sequence diagram.
why.d: Wrong. Conversion is an installation approach.

prompt: True or false: the object-oriented design activities are strictly linear, and gaps found later are never fed back.
explanation: They are ITERATIVE: a sequence diagram may reveal that a class needs an operation nobody listed, and that goes back into earlier steps.

why.true: Wrong. The text calls them iterative.

prompt: What does the course text say UML is, and what is it NOT?

options.text: It is the industry-standard notation for object-oriented analysis and design; it is not a method in itself
It is a development methodology; it is not a notation
It is a programming language; it is not a diagram
It is a database product; it is not a model

explanation: UML is a common visual language that different object-oriented methods can use. Notation, not method.

why.c: Wrong. UML is a modelling notation.
why.d: Wrong. UML is not a database.

prompt: Match each UML diagram with its group in the course text.
explanation: Structural: class, component, deployment. Behavioural: use case, sequence, activity, state chart, collaboration.

prompt: Which of these is a STRUCTURAL UML diagram in the course text?
explanation: Structural diagrams describe static structure: class, component and deployment diagrams.

prompt: True or false: behavioural diagrams describe how the system behaves over time, including how objects change state.
explanation: Behavioural diagrams cover interaction, flow of control and state changes: use case, sequence, activity, state chart and collaboration.

why.true: Correct. That is the behavioural group.
why.false: Wrong. The text describes behavioural diagrams exactly so.

prompt: In object-oriented analysis and design, what does each object manage?

options.text: Its own data, called state, and its own behaviour, called operations

explanation: Each object manages its own state and operations; the system is the objects messaging each other.

why.a: Correct. Its own state and operations.
why.b: Wrong. Not what the text says.
why.c: Wrong. Not what the text says.
why.d: Wrong. Control is spread across objects sending messages.
